config.title: Sliding Window Maximum (Deque)

intro.title: Sliding Window Maximum (Deque)
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that finds the maximum value in every possible subarray of a fixed size within a given array, using the sliding window technique. You will learn how to implement this efficiently using a deque (double-ended queue) to track potential maximum candidates as the window moves. The core programming concepts involve array traversal, queue operations, and maintaining optimal data structures for performance. You will work with JavaScript arrays and implement custom logic to manage the deque, focusing on time complexity optimization for this common algorithmic pattern.
intro.usecase: The sliding window maximum algorithm is essential for real-time data analysis in financial dashboards, where traders need to track the highest stock price within a moving time window. It powers performance monitoring tools that display peak server load or maximum network latency over rolling intervals. This pattern also enables efficient filtering in data visualization systems, such as showing the highest temperature or maximum sales value across consecutive time periods in analytics applications.

objectives: Construct a deque data structure using arrays to maintain window indices
Initialize pointers and variables to track the sliding window boundaries
Manipulate the deque by removing indices that fall outside the current window
Apply comparison logic to maintain decreasing order of values in the deque
Integrate deque operations within a loop to process each element in the array
Render the maximum values for each window position in the output array
Configure the algorithm to handle varying window sizes and input arrays

content.body: Imagine you're looking through a moving camera lens at a long line of numbers. You can only see a few numbers at a time through your lens. Your job is to find the largest number in each view as the lens slides along. This is the sliding window maximum lesson—a clever way to track extremes in a moving segment of data.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Explain what a sliding window is in array lessons.
• Identify when to expand and shrink the window.
• Implement a deque (double-ended queue) to efficiently track maximum values.
• Solve the sliding window maximum lesson in one pass.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start small. Look at this array: [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7]. Imagine you have a window that shows only 3 numbers at a time. Starting at the beginning, what's the largest number in the first window (positions 0-2)?
content.title: Try it

content.body: Now slide your window one position to the right. The window now shows positions 1-3: [3, -1, -3]. What's the maximum now? Notice how the window moved—the leftmost number left the view, and a new number entered on the right.
content.title: Slide it

content.body: Slide one more time to positions 2-4: [-1, -3, 5]. What's the maximum? You're manually checking each window's contents. This works for small windows, but what if the window was size 100 and the array had 10,000 numbers?
content.title: Keep going

content.body: You just performed a brute-force approach: for each window position, you looked at all elements inside to find the maximum. This involves repeatedly checking the same numbers as windows overlap.
content.title: What you did

content.body: With large arrays and windows, checking every element in every window becomes extremely inefficient. We need a smarter way that avoids re-examining numbers unnecessarily. The key is maintaining knowledge about which numbers matter as the window moves.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Think of the window as a moving segment of the array. We expand the window to the right as we move forward. We shrink from the left when elements leave the window. The challenge is efficiently tracking the maximum within this dynamic segment without scanning all elements each time.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Picture a highlight that slides along the array, growing on the right side and shrinking on the left as it moves.

content.body:
We'll use a deque (double-ended queue) to store indices of array elements. The deque will maintain candidates for the current maximum in decreasing order. When the window slides:
1. Remove indices from the front that are now outside the window.
2. Remove indices from the back for elements smaller than the new element.
3. Add the new element's index to the back.
4. The front always holds the index of the current maximum.
This way, we track the maximum in O(1) time as the window moves.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Initialize an empty deque and result array.
2. Iterate through each element in the array.
3. Remove from front: if front index is outside current window, pop it.
4. Remove from back: while back element is smaller than current element, pop it.
5. Add current index to back of deque.
6. Once window size is reached, record deque front's value as maximum.
7. Continue until end of array.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up function and variables
steps.instruction: Create the function skeleton and initialize the deque and result array. We'll use a simple array as our deque.
steps.hint: Define a function that takes nums and k parameters. Create empty arrays for deque and result.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function declaration with empty deque and result variables.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great start! You've set up the basic structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you declare both the deque and result variables.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to create variables for the deque and result array inside the function.

steps.title: Iterate through the array
steps.instruction: Add a loop to go through each element. We'll need the current index to manage the window boundaries.
steps.hint: Use a standard for loop from 0 to nums.length.
steps.expectedOutcome: A for loop that iterates through all indices of nums.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now we can process each element.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Make sure your loop goes through all indices of the nums array.
steps.feedbackWrong: You need a loop that iterates from 0 to nums.length.

steps.title: Remove outdated indices from front
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, check if the front of the deque is outside the current window. The window starts at i-k+1. Remove from front if deque[0] < i-k+1.
steps.hint: Use while loop and shift() to remove from front when index is too small.
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that removes indices from deque front when they're outside current window.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good attempt. Make sure you're comparing deque[0] with i-k+1.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: we need to remove indices that are less than i-k+1 from the front of deque.

steps.title: Maintain decreasing order in deque
steps.instruction: Now, remove from the back of deque while the current element is greater than the element at the back index. This keeps the deque in decreasing order.
steps.hint: Use while loop and pop() when nums[i] > nums[deque[deque.length-1]].
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that pops from deque back while current element is larger than back element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! This maintains the decreasing order property.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Check if nums[i] is greater than the element at the back index.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to remove elements from the back while they're smaller than the current element.

steps.title: Add current index and record maximum
steps.instruction: Add the current index to deque. Then, if we've processed at least k elements (i >= k-1), record the maximum (front of deque) to result.
steps.hint: Push i to deque. Check if i >= k-1, then push nums[deque[0]] to result.
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that adds current index and records maximum when window is full.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've completed the core logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress. Don't forget to add the index and check if window is complete.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to: 1) push i to deque, 2) check if i >= k-1 to record the maximum.

steps.title: Return result and test
steps.instruction: Complete the function by returning the result array. Add a test case to verify it works.
steps.hint: Simply return result at the end. You can add a console.log to test.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function returns result array and logs [3,3,5,5,6,7].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you're returning the result array.
steps.feedbackWrong: Don't forget to return the result array at the end of the function.

content.body:
Congratulations! You've implemented the sliding window maximum algorithm using a deque. Remember these key points:
• The window is a moving segment that expands right and shrinks left.
• The deque maintains candidate maximums in decreasing order.
• We remove from front when indices leave the window.
• We remove from back when smaller elements become irrelevant.
• This approach runs in O(n) time—much faster than brute force!
This pattern applies to many sliding window lessons where you need to track extremes or aggregates efficiently.
